text: DORA stands for DevOps Research and Assessment — the research team that spent years surveying tens of thousands of software teams and found four specific, measurable metrics that reliably separate high-performing organizations from low-performing ones. Those findings were published in the book Accelerate and the annual State of DevOps report, and they're the first thing a platform team should instrument, because they're the most evidence-backed proxy anyone has found for whether an organization is actually good at shipping software.

The four metrics split into two pairs. Deployment frequency and lead time for changes measure throughput: how often you ship, and how long a commit takes to reach production. Change failure rate and time to restore service measure stability: what percentage of deploys degrade production, and how fast you recover. Lead time directly reflects your pipeline design from earlier chapters — every manual approval gate and flaky test suite shows up right here.

None of this requires a new tool bolted onto the side. Deployment frequency is a count of successful production deploys over a time window, straight from your CI/CD system or GitOps controller. Lead time is the deploy timestamp minus the first commit timestamp on the merged pull request. Change failure rate is failed deploys divided by total deploys, where failed means a rollback, hotfix, or tagged incident. Time to restore is incident resolved time minus incident detected time.

The State of DevOps report sorts organizations into four tiers. Elite performers deploy on demand, multiple times a day. High performers deploy somewhere between daily and weekly. Medium performers land between weekly and monthly. Low performers deploy less than once every six months — and at that cadence, every release is necessarily a large, high-risk batch of change, almost by definition, whether or not anyone intended it that way.

Here's the counter-intuitive part: throughput and stability aren't in tension. Elite teams don't trade speed for safety — they score well on all four metrics at once. Small changes, automated pipelines, declarative GitOps state, and progressive delivery with automated rollback all shrink the size and risk of each change, which improves throughput and stability simultaneously. That's the mechanism this entire course has been building toward, not a coincidence in the survey data.

These four metrics tell you a lot about delivery performance, but notice what they don't measure anywhere: whether the developers generating all that activity can actually stand working on the platform day to day. That's next — measuring developer experience itself, not just the system's uptime.
